SK3007 A Task that uses a using resource is returned instead of awaited

A non-async method returns a task built from a using variable, so the resource is disposed before the task completes.

CategoryAsync
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since1.2
ReSharperReturnOfTaskProducedByUsingVariable (resharper_return_of_task_produced_by_using_variable_highlighting)

Why

Returning a task out of a using disposes the resource at the return, not when the task finishes. The task is then running against a disposed stream, connection or scope, and what the caller gets is an ObjectDisposedException from somewhere with no visible connection to the using — or, worse, a task that completes because the operation had already finished, so the bug reproduces only under load. Awaiting inside the block is the whole repair, and because the method already returns a task, adding async changes its signature not at all.

Example

Instead of:

Task<string> ReadAsync(string path) {
    using (var reader = new StreamReader(path)) {
        return reader.ReadToEndAsync();
    }
}

Write:

async Task<string> ReadAsync(string path) {
    using (var reader = new StreamReader(path)) {
        return await reader.ReadToEndAsync();
    }
}

When it does not fire

The rule fires only where the repair is provably complete, which is a much narrower shape than the bug. ⚠ The returned expression must name the `using` variable. A task that does not mention the resource may still be wrong — a using that is a lock scope is the case — but the rule cannot prove it, and a rule that guesses about ownership is a rule that reports the correct code around it. ⚠ Every `return` in the method is rewritten, or none is. Adding async makes the method's other returns need await too, so the rule collects them all and withholds the finding when any of them returns something that is not a task of the method's own type — a null, a default, or a differently-typed task. ⚠ Only ordinary methods and local functions with block bodies, whose declared return type is exactly Task, Task<T>, ValueTask or ValueTask<T>, and which are not already async, not abstract, not partial and not iterators. Lambdas are excluded because async goes in a different place in each of their spellings. The fix is unsafe by declaration: an async method reports a synchronous throw as a faulted task rather than throwing at the call, which is a real difference for a caller that does not await immediately.
